claims.text: An approach integrating chemical-disorder descriptors, machine learning, and lattice-dynamics calculations can accurately identify single-phase HEAs with ultralow phonon thermal conductivity.
Mass and force-constant fluctuations are the reason the integrated approach can identify low-thermal-conductivity HEAs.
The target materials are chemically disordered, single-phase FCC or BCC solid solutions similar to FeCoCrMnNi.
Such HEAs possess inherent chemical lattice distortions.
The proposed framework combines machine learning with first-principles or lattice-dynamics calculations.
Configurational entropy, atomic-mass variance, and lattice-distortion parameters are suitable descriptors for the proposed prediction task.
The predictions apply at room and elevated temperatures while the alloys remain stable single-phase solid solutions without phase separation or significant grain-boundary effects.
Chemical disorder produces mass and force-constant fluctuations.
Mass and force-constant fluctuations disrupt long-range phonon propagation.
Local lattice distortions and atomic-size mismatch scatter phonons in HEAs.
Increased phonon scattering reduces phonon lifetimes and thereby lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
The cited PbSnTeSe computational study found very low lattice thermal conductivity using first-principles calculations, on-the-fly machine learning, and transport calculations.
The proposed model will identify compositions whose phonon thermal conductivity is approximately 20–30% lower than that of compositions identified by conventional prediction schemes.
Current conventional methods rely predominantly on binary-phase extrapolations or thermodynamic descriptors and omit explicit atomic-scale disorder effects.
The approach is primarily applicable to single-phase, chemically disordered HEAs.
The approach may be unreliable for alloys containing substantial secondary phases, intermetallic compounds, or non-equilibrium microstructures.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant, reproducible improvement of approximately 20% together with the predicted decrease in phonon lifetime would falsify the hypothesis.
